teaser: A Tahitian greeting, a Catholic prayer and a pose borrowed from a temple in Java.
review_notes:
“Ia ora na” as the standard Tahitian greeting today; Gauguin's spelling “Ia orana”.
Letter to Daniel de Monfreid of March 1892 describing the angel with yellow wings, Mary and Jesus as Tahitians, and saying he was rather pleased with it (paraphrased, not quoted).
Pose of the two worshippers taken from a photograph of a relief at Borobudur, Java, which Gauguin owned.
Gauguin offered the painting to the Musée du Luxembourg after his return in 1893 and it was refused.
Met credit line: Bequest of Sam A. Lewisohn, 1951.
Dimensions about 114 x 88 cm.
Quote “little world of friends” (un petit monde de camarades, letter to Odilon Redon, 1890).
Identification of the red fruit as fei (mountain plantains) and of the wooden stand as a fata, an offering platform.

lesson.text: Step off a plane in Tahiti today and the first thing you hear is “Ia ora na”. It means hello. It is printed on welcome signs and said in every shop. Now look at the yellow panel at the bottom of this painting from 1891: the same words, followed by a name. Hello, Mary.

Gauguin was translating the opening of the best-known Catholic prayer, “Hail Mary”, into the language of the island he had just moved to. Then he did the same with the image itself. He took one of the oldest subjects in European art and recast every role.
In a letter to a friend he listed the cast: an angel, two women, and Mary carrying Jesus, all of them Tahitian. Mary and the child are easy to pick out on the right. The angel is another matter.
An angel with yellow wings is announcing the scene. It is half hidden. Where?

spots.title: The angel
spots.text: Behind a flowering bush, a figure in pink and blue bends its dark head. Two yellow wings spread out on either side. Gauguin tucks the one supernatural being into the foliage like something glimpsed.

lesson.text: In a Renaissance altarpiece the angel would stand in the middle, lit and unmistakable. Here it is the last thing you see. The fruit, the women and the mountains all have more presence. The miracle is folded into an ordinary morning.

Gauguin sailed to Tahiti with a trunk of photographs: Egyptian tomb paintings, Greek friezes, Japanese prints, temple carvings. He called this collection his “little world of friends” and borrowed from it for years.

One of those photographs showed stone reliefs from Borobudur, a huge Buddhist temple on the island of Java. Keep that in mind as the camera moves from the two women in the middle to the mother and child.

lesson.title: Borrowed holiness
lesson.text: Three signs of the sacred, from three different traditions.

spots.title: Hands pressed together
spots.text: The two women walk forward with joined palms. The gesture and the slightly stiff, sideways poses come from the Javanese temple carvings, where figures greet the Buddha this way.

spots.title: Two thin halos
spots.text: A fine gold ring circles Mary's head, and another the child's. This is the Christian sign for a holy person, drawn so lightly that it almost disappears against the trees.

spots.title: A red pareo
spots.text: Mary wears no blue cloak. She has the wrapped cotton cloth of the island, red with white flowers, and carries her son on one shoulder, as mothers there did.

lesson.text: Gauguin mixes a Catholic prayer, Buddhist poses and Tahitian daily life in one picture. He is suggesting that the sacred is not owned by any single place or people.

That idea did not come from nowhere. Tahiti in 1891 was a deeply Christian island, with churches in every district and hymns sung in Tahitian. Gauguin went looking for ancient gods and mostly found Sunday services. This painting is one of the few where he paints the religion that was really there.
He was proud of it. It was the first large canvas he completed in Tahiti, about 114 by 88 centimeters (45 by 35 inches), and he signed and dated it at the lower right, opposite the title.
Back in Paris in 1893, Gauguin offered this painting as a gift to the Musée du Luxembourg, then France's museum for living artists. The museum turned it down.

There is one more offering to look at. At the very front, pushed almost into your lap, sits a low wooden stand piled with fruit. In Polynesia food was laid on platforms like this for the gods. Gauguin sets it where a European painter would put flowers at the Virgin's feet.

spots.title: Bananas
spots.text: A bowl of pale yellow bananas, each one outlined and shaded like a small sculpture. They are the nearest thing to you in the whole picture.

spots.title: Red plantains
spots.text: These orange-red bunches are fei, mountain plantains that grow in Tahiti's highlands and are eaten cooked. Their color answers the red of Mary's cloth across the picture.

spots.title: The title
spots.text: IA ORANA MARIA, painted in capitals on a yellow strip. Gauguin often wrote Tahitian titles on his canvases, knowing buyers in Paris would not understand them.

spots.title: Flowering tree
spots.text: A tree covered in white and pink blossoms rises behind the worshippers. Its dark leaves are painted as flat, interlocking shapes, close to a pattern on fabric.

spots.title: Blue and white cloths
spots.text: One woman wears deep blue with yellow flowers, the other plain white. With Mary's red, the three cloths give the picture its main chord of color.

spots.title: The violet path
spots.text: The ground the women walk on is lilac and mauve. Gauguin picks colors for their mood and for how they sit beside each other, not for accuracy.

lesson.text: The fruit, the path and the cloths all push the same way: colors laid side by side in flat areas, each with a firm edge. Shadows are nearly absent. Gauguin wanted a painting to work first as an arrangement, the way music works before you know what the song is about.
The painting crossed two oceans to reach Paris, then one more to reach New York. It entered the Metropolitan Museum of Art in 1951, as part of a collector's bequest.
So the greeting keeps traveling. Painted on a strip of yellow in 1891, refused by one museum, treasured by another, and still said out loud every day in the place where Gauguin first learned it.

quiz.question: What does “Ia orana Maria” mean?
quiz.explanation: It is the opening of the Catholic prayer, put into Tahitian.

quiz.question: Where is the angel in the painting?
options: In the center, between the two women
Floating in the sky above Mary
On the left, half hidden behind a flowering bush
quiz.explanation: Gauguin tucks the yellow-winged angel into the foliage.

quiz.question: Where did Gauguin find the poses of the two praying women?
options: In a photograph of temple reliefs from Java
In an Italian altarpiece he saw in Rome
quiz.explanation: He owned a photograph of the carvings at Borobudur and borrowed from it.

quiz.question: What marks Mary and the child as holy?
options: A beam of light from the clouds
Thin gold halos around their heads
quiz.explanation: Each has a fine gold ring around the head.

quiz.question: What happened when Gauguin offered the painting to the Musée du Luxembourg?
options: It was bought for a record price
It was hung in the entrance hall
quiz.explanation: The museum turned the gift down.

facts.text: Mary wears the traditional blue cloak of European paintings.
facts.explanation: She wears a red Tahitian pareo with white flowers.

facts.text: Gauguin traveled with a collection of photographs of art from many cultures.
facts.explanation: He took a trunk of them to Tahiti and borrowed poses from them.

facts.text: Tahiti was largely untouched by Christianity when Gauguin arrived.
facts.explanation: It was a deeply Christian island with churches in every district.
